Zig posts the strongest location and excerpt evidence of any language measured -- 8 of 8 on both D1 and D2, the only language to reproduce the source line and caret for the runtime probe as well -- but the other four indicators fail: D3 is 0 of 8 (no codes or rule names anywhere), D4 is 4 of 8, D5 is 0 of 8, and there is no documented structured-diagnostics mode for D6. Not the level above (Basic, 3): no third indicator reaches its threshold. Not the level below (Minimal, 0 or 1): two indicators are satisfied at full strength, and all 8 probes emit a diagnostic -- Zig is one of only two languages (with Rust) where every probe produces one. AUDITOR NOTE: this is the clearest case in this metric of the six-equal-indicators count compressing a strong profile on two axes into a low level; it is reported as the frozen rubric computes it.

cross_language_consistency_note: Same-meaning-per-level was enforced four ways. (1) IDENTICAL PROBE SEMANTICS: one source program per probe per language, written to the same eight frozen requirements, using each language's ordinary construct rather than its safest one -- ordinary indexing (v[i], not vector::at) for DIAG-8, an ordinary local for DIAG-5, an ordinary member call for DIAG-6. DIAG-8's index is returned by a function in all ten so no compiler can constant-fold it into a compile-time error. (2) ONE FROZEN COMMAND PER LANGUAGE: the frozen_diagnostic_configuration row verbatim, verified against the rubric text; no language had two commands tried and the better output kept. (3) UNIFORM INDICATOR TESTS, fixed before counting and applied to all ten: D1 requires a NUMERIC column or offset in the printed text (a caret alone is D2, never D1) -- this is what puts Python and Java at 0 of 8; D2 requires a reproduced source line or caret/excerpt; D3 requires a token from a fixed enumeration of identifiers that is documented under E2 -- credited for Quidra's error[CODE] table, Rust's E#### plus lint names, and Python's/Java's/Kotlin's documented exception class names, refused for TypeScript because no official documentation of TS#### was found; D4 requires the offending identifier or BOTH conflicting types to be NAMED IN THE MESSAGE TEXT, not merely underlined by the caret -- this is what separates C++/Go/Java/Kotlin/Swift ('no matching function for call to add', 'no value passed for parameter b') from Rust/Zig/Quidra ('this function takes 2 arguments', 'expected 2 argument(s)', 'Missing required argument.') on DIAG-3, and Zig from everyone else on DIAG-5; D5 requires a line stating what to do about the defect, excluding tooling hints about obtaining more output (RUST_BACKTRACE, -freference-trace) -- no language reaches 6 of 8 on D5 under either reading, so this choice changes no score; D6 requires a documented flag plus a successful parse, and the parser is not required to be first-party. (4) TTY SYMMETRY CHECK: tsc suppresses its source excerpt when stdout is not a TTY, so every language whose piped output showed no excerpt (Quidra, Go) and one control (Java) was re-run under a pty with script(1). Quidra and Go emit no excerpt either way; tsc's documented default is --pretty:true, so TypeScript was scored from the pty capture. PAIRWISE RE-READ of the ten assignments: the four 20s (Python D2+D3; TypeScript D1+D2; Kotlin D1+D2; Zig D1+D2) differ in which indicators hold but agree on the count. The two 40s (Quidra D1+D3+D6; Go D1+D4+D6) likewise. The three 60s (C++ D1+D2+D4+D6; Rust D1+D2+D3+D6; Swift D1+D2+D4+D6) trade D3 against D4 evenly; C++ and Swift have observably identical indicator sets and receive the same level, as required. Java at 0 is the only language with a single satisfied indicator, and it is the only one failing BOTH D1 (no column anywhere) and D3 (no compile-time identifier) while also missing D4 by one probe. No two languages with the same observable evidence received different levels, and no two with clearly different evidence received the same level for the same reasons.
fairness_statement: Quidra was measured last under the same eight probes, the same indicator tests and the same E1/E2 sources as the other nine. No age, maturity, incumbency or potential adjustment was applied in either direction. Quidra's real advantages were scored normally (a documented 85-entry diagnostic code table gives it D3 at 7 of 8, which C++, Go, Java, Kotlin, Swift and Zig do not satisfy, and quidra check --json gives it D6), and its real deficits were scored normally (D2 at 0 of 8 -- no source excerpt or caret for any probe, the joint-worst D2 result with Go; D5 at 0 of 8; D4 at 4 of 8). The established languages' real advantages were scored normally too: clang's SARIF, rustc's error index and JSON output, swiftc's serialized diagnostics and go build -json were all credited on execution, not discounted.
limitations: TypeScript D3 is the single most consequential judgement in this metric (crediting it moves TypeScript 20 -> 40). tsc emits stable TS#### codes on every failing probe, but no documentation of the code scheme or of the specific codes TS2304/TS2322/TS2554/TS1005/TS2339 was found at the TypeScript official_docs_root: the handbook page 'Understanding Errors' (HTTP 200, 199751 bytes) contains no code index and no TS#### in prose, and grep -oE 'TS[0-9]{4}' returned zero matches on both the TSConfig reference (809189 bytes) and the compiler-options page (240063 bytes). microsoft/TypeScript's diagnosticMessages.json does carry the codes, but it is a source file under E3, whereas D3's supporting_source_id is E2. Scored NOT SATISFIED on the frozen wording. An auditor who reads 'official documentation' as including the official repository should raise TypeScript to 40; no other language's score turns on that reading.

Swift D6 was verified with llvm-bcanalyzer 22.1.5 from Homebrew LLVM, which is not part of the Swift toolchain. The .dia file is an LLVM bitstream, not JSON or SARIF; it was credited under the indicator's 'or equivalent' clause because the flag is documented in swiftc --help and the output parsed successfully, recovering file, line, column and message. Had no bitstream reader existed on this host the indicator would have been recorded unverified and therefore unsatisfied, which would move Swift from 60 to 40.

Go D6 and C++ D6 carry recorded caveats that did not change their scores: Go's JSON envelope carries the diagnostic as an unstructured text string in an 'Output' field rather than as structured fields, and clang prints 'diagnostic formatting in SARIF mode is currently unstable [-Wsarif-format-unstable]'. Both were credited because the indicator's stated test -- documented flag, executed on DIAG-2, output parsed successfully -- is met.

javac's diagnostics were captured in the host's default locale (ja_JP). An English rendering was additionally captured with -J-Duser.language=en for auditability. Message language affects no indicator (all six test structure: column number, excerpt, identifier, named entities, fix line, output format), and both captures were checked against each other. The scored capture is the frozen command in the host's default environment.

Java's frozen run recipe names entry class Main; the probe entry classes are Diag1..Diag8 because javac ties the file name to the class. This is an entry-class-name adaptation only, with no flag change, and affects only which class name appears in the DIAG-8 stack trace.

DIAG-7 for Python could not be given a semantically enforced form. The probe requires a function declared to return an integer that returns a string; Python's `-> int` annotation is the direct translation but is not enforced at run time and -X dev does not check it, so the program runs clean and the probe counts as emitting no diagnostic. Unlike DIAG-2, the frozen DIAG-7 requirement carries no 'nearest equivalent' fallback clause, so none was invented. Python's no-diagnostic probes total 2 (DIAG-5, DIAG-7), below the 3-probe clause that would force the 0 level, so this did not change Python's score.

No first-party static type checker (mypy, pyright) was run for Python and no linter (clippy, golangci-lint, ktlint, ESLint) for any language: the frozen_diagnostic_configuration fixes exactly one compile-or-check command per language and none of those rows names a separate checker. This constrains Python and, to a lesser degree, TypeScript, and is a property of the frozen configuration rather than of this scoring pass.

D5 was evaluated under the reading that tooling hints about obtaining more output (Rust's RUST_BACKTRACE note, Zig's -freference-trace note) are not 'actionable lines stating what to do' about the defect. Under the opposite reading Rust would reach 3 of 8 and Zig 4 of 8 on D5; neither reaches the 6-of-8 threshold, so no score in this metric depends on that reading.
All ten languages were examined under both E1 and E2. There is no language for which evidence was unobtainable under a source another language was scored under.
